title: Viral vectors for opto-electrode recording and photometry-based imaging of oxytocin neurons in anesthetized and socially interacting rats
protocol: Insert silicon probe electrode into a single-axis optic fiber integrated with a microdrive.
Mount tungsten-wire tetrodes surrounding an optic fiber in the middle using VersaDrive-8 Optical.
Implant two ground/reference screws in the posterior part of the skull during surgery.
Drill craniotomy holes above the target brain areas for implantation.
Seal the implantation hole and the naked opto-electrode shank with pre-heated wax.
Apply a 3D-printed plastic cover around the probe implantation site and fix it with UV glue.
Suture the skin after sealing the implantation site.
Place a copper mesh around the whole implanted drive and solder grounding wires to the copper mesh to form a mini-faraday cage.
Align the probe tip to Bregma zero point.
Move the probe above the target coordinates.
Slowly implant the probe half way before the microdrive base touches the skull.
Fix the microdrive base on the skull with UV-glue.
Apply dental cement over the fixed microdrive base.
Make the incision on the skin at least 2 cm long.
Use four bulldog skin clamps to ensure adequate exposure of the Bregma–Lambda region.
Clean the skull around the implantation site with 2% hydrogen peroxide (H2O2).
Make six holes (0.5 mm diameter) in the skull around the implantation site using a high-speed drill.
Install two stainless-steel screws pre-soldered with silver wires (ground and reference) in the two most caudal holes.
Install regular stainless-steel screws in the remaining four holes.
Cover the six screws with a thin layer of UV glue for better anchoring on the skull surface.
Use micro-drills to enlarge the PVN injection hole for the implant.
Remove debris with a rubber suction bulb.
Penetrate the dura with a fine needle or insect pin.
If bleeding occurs, apply gentle pressure with a micro hemostatic sponge.
Clean tissue hyperplasia around the craniotomy hole with sterilized PBS solution.
Remove excess tissue or protective gel using fine tweezers.
Enlarge the craniotomy hole to obtain a diameter of 0.5–1 mm.
Propel the microdrive to extend the pre-mounted opto-probe or opto-tetrodes up to half of its full length.
Attach the microdrive to the stereotaxic arm with an adaptor.
Verify that the opto-electrode shank is perfectly aligned vertically on the stereotaxic frame in all directions.
Loosen lateral optic fiber fixation screws before propelling the probes.
Mount the microdrive with the opto-electrode onto the stereotaxic arm with an adapter.
Repeat the stereotaxic calibration of the skull with respect to Bregma using the tip of the opto-electrode.
Position the shank above the craniotomy hole (AP: −1.8 mm, ML 0.35 mm for PVN).
Position the probe medial and the optic fiber lateral to the skull midline.
Ensure the opto-electrode shank fits in the craniotomy hole.
Slowly insert the opto-electrode into the brain tissue at 10 μm/s.
Pause and wash with PBS for 1 minute if bleeding occurs during insertion.
Retract electrodes from brain tissue, wash thoroughly with PBS if bending occurs upon entering the brain.
Adjust electrode position by 100 μm anterior or posterior before re-attempting implantation.
Apply wax prior to fixing the drive base on the skull when working with tetrodes.
Seal the probe shank and implantation hole with heated wax.
Place solid wax around the electrodes.
Melt wax using a soldering gun (80°C–100°C) or in a beaker and draw into a syringe.
Quickly apply melted wax to the electrodes implantation site before it turns solid again.
Remove any excess wax around the craniotomy hole carefully.
Fix the base of the microdrive onto the rat’s skull with UV glue (3M RelyXUnicem 2).
Apply dental cement (Paladur, Heraeus Kulzer; interior layer 1:2, outer layer 1:1 liquid:solid component ratio) around the microdrive base and six anchor screws.
Mount the Omnetics connector onto the microdrive after the dental cement has solidified.
Prepare a custom-made square-shaped copper mesh to protect the microdrive and opto-electrodes from physical damage.
Solder the wires from ground and reference screws to the copper mesh to build a mini-faraday cage around the implanted head-stage.
Seal the copper mesh all around the microdrive with solder.
Fix the copper mesh to the skull with dental cement.
Prevent leakage of soldering material onto the rat’s skin.
Firmly solder ground wires to the copper mesh.
Secure the ground wires and dental cement to the skull with dental cement.
Let the dental cement dry for 10 minutes.
Place the rat in a heated recovery cage without any objects that can damage implants during awakening.
After recovery, place the rat in a single-housing cage with a high ceiling.
Monitor the health status of the rat every day for one week after implantation.
Administer analgesic via drinking water (e.g., Dafalgan 500 mg/L).
Return to normal behavior typically occurs 3 days after surgery.
If the rat continues to frequently scratch the surgical site, administer additional analgesic (e.g., Rapidocain 30 mg/kg i.p.).
Handle the rat for 15 min/day starting from day 3 following implantation until day 7 for habituation to the connecting procedure.
Secure the Neuronexus oDrive with lateral screws.
Fix the optic fiber ferrule and mount the tetrodes to the microdrive independently.
Turn on the laser 30 minutes before starting the recording to preheat the system.
Adjust the laser power to have a stable output of 10–20 mW/mm² after coupling the optic patch cord to the laser.
Measure the power of each optic fiber in advance with an optical power meter.
Gently lock the rat’s head with one hand.
Connect the optic fiber to the fiber patch cord and the Omnetics connector.
Align the connector and pre-amplifier correctly with the printed logo “Omnetics” on the same side.
Attach the recording cable to the recording system.
Connect the fiber patch cord to the laser.
Place the connected rat into a clean and empty cage.
Handle the animal gently to reduce stress.
Wait for the rat to calm down if it shows signs of stress during handling.
Optionally, lightly anesthetize the rat in the isoflurane chamber before connecting cables.
Set parameters on the triggering device to activate the laser with 10 ms pulses at different inter-pulse intervals (1 Hz, 5 Hz, or 10 Hz).
Turn on the data acquisition system.
Link the laser TTL output to the digital input of the DAQ board.
Start the electrophysiology recording and stimulation sequence.
Visualize the light-evoked response of the recorded single units online in the raster mode aligned to the laser TTL signals.
Check if some neurons are activated by the light pulses.
Analyze sorted spikes in a peri-stimulus time histogram (PSTH) aligned to the onset of the light pulses offline.
Label only units that show a clear increase (+3 standard deviations compared to the average of 100 ms during pre-stimulation, peak response within 10 ms delay) as ChR2-expressing OT neurons.
Refer to ‘problem 5’ for potential solutions if no action potentials are detected with the recording electrodes in the target region (PVN).
Refer to ‘problem 6’ for potential solutions if no neurons respond to the blue laser stimuli or have a long delay and/or jittered response.
Save the channel number and firing properties of optically responding cells for easier identification in analysis.
Convert the channel arrangement illustrated in the channel map provided by the manufacturer when using silicon probes, depending on the type of adaptor and preamplifier used.
Check carefully the channel arrangement before implanting the probe by inserting it slowly into sterile PBS solution.
Visualize the noise level of each channel in real time on the recording acquisition system.
When electrodes are inserted into PBS solution, observe a decrease in the noise level of the corresponding channel due to higher conductivity compared to air.
If no units were found responding to laser stimuli, propel the microdrive 50–100 μm and wait a few hours before re-doing the steps above.
Do not propel the microdrive more than 200 μm per day.
Bring the experimental rat and the stimulus rats into the recording room at least 30 min prior to the recording, to allow the rats to habituate to the new environment.
Place the experimental rat into the recording chamber.
Start the recording session, synchronizing electrophysiology recording and video camera.
Allow the rat to freely explore the open field arena for 10 minutes.
Remove the rat from the arena and place it in an empty clean cage for 15 minutes.
Place the experimental rat and a conspecific naïve rat into opposite corners of the recording chamber simultaneously.
Let both rats interact for 10 minutes.
Thoroughly clean the arena with 70% ethanol followed by distilled water before each experiment.
Use low illumination (< 20 Lux) in the recording chamber to avoid stress for the animals.
Track the rat’s locomotion using automated tracking software.
Manually annotate social interaction events during the session.
Remove both rats from the recording chamber and place them in separate cages.
Repeat steps similar to those described at the end of the recording session to confirm opto-tagged neuron identity.
Attach a temporary opto-electrode and its connectors to the stereotaxic arm.
Connect the preamplifier and optic fiber patch cord to the probe immediately after attachment.
Implant two screws on the rat’s skull for grounding and referencing purposes.
Do not implant anchor screws.
Connect the probe’s ground pin with the wire attached to the ground screw.
Connect the probe’s reference pin with the wire attached to the reference screw.
Periodically apply sterilized PBS solution on the rat's skull to keep the brain moist during implantation and recording.
Monitor the rat’s breathing rate throughout the procedure.
Ground all electronic devices in the setup, including the stereotaxic frame, heating plate, and laser generators, to the faraday cage.
Check the basal noise level of the signal after applying band-pass filter (<25 μV) before implanting and recording.
Retract the opto-electrode at 200 μm/min for the first 5 minutes, then at 2 mm/min until fully retracted.
Wash the opto-electrode with PBS.
Redo the implantation procedure.
Perform an acute recording of opto-tagged OT neurons while delivering external sensory stimulation such as 'airpuffs' to the rat.
Carefully retract the opto-electrode after recording.
Unplug the connectors following recording.
Wash the probe according to the protocol described below.
Gold-plate the probe after repeated usage to maintain impedance between 0.3–0.5 MΩ.
Sacrifice the rat after recording.
Perfuse the rat with PFA (4%).
Extract the brain to verify the implantation site.
Rinse the silicon probe with distilled water immediately after withdrawing it from brain tissue.

Soak only the silicon shank of the probe in a protein-dissolving detergent (e.g., enzyme cleaner AN000689 from Thomas Recording, 1 g/50 mL of distilled water) or diluted surgical instrument detergent (e.g., EmPower from Metrex, 1:128 in 20°C–40°C water).
Sterilize the probe with isopropyl alcohol (e.g., 70% IPA) for no more than 15 seconds after protein dissolving.
Avoid using ultrasonic cleaners and do not autoclave probes to prevent damage.
Inject viral vector designed to express GCaMP6s in OT neurons (rAAV-OTp-GCaMP6s) into the PVN.
Wait three to four weeks after injection for expression of GCaMP6s.
Implant an optic fiber above the PVN to collect fluorescent signals from OT neural ensemble.
Record signal from optic fiber during surgery if optimization is needed.
Follow the initial steps for surgery preparation as described in the viral injection section.
Prepare a clean and exposed skull for implantation of fiber optic cannulas.
Perform the craniotomy in a circular shape, 1 mm diameter, above the target region using a high-speed drill.
Be careful when drilling near blood vessels.
Clean the craniotomy region with 2% H2O2 and let it dry for 1 minute.
Retract the fiber tip if blood contacts it.
Clean the fiber tip with ethanol (70%) if contaminated by blood or exudates.
Connect the fiber tip to the fiber photometry recording setup using an optic patch cord (mono fiber optics patch cord, Doric Lenses).
Visualize the output fluorescence from the fiber tip.
Connect the implantable fiber cannula (Thorlabs, CFMXD10, CFMC54L10) to the fiber patch cord with quick release interconnectors (Thorlabs ADAF2, ADAL3) or mating sleeves.
Attach the optic fiber and patch cord to the stereotaxic holder.
Ensure the optic fiber is perfectly aligned vertically on all sides with respect to the frame.
Slowly insert the fiber at 10 mm/s until it is approximately 100 μm above the target region (for PVN, DV −7.9 mm).
Observe an increase in fluorescent signal as the fiber approaches the GCaMP6s sensor expression site.
Fine-tune the depth of insertion to maximize the fluorescence signal.
Withdraw the cannula by 0.3 mm for every 1 mm of insertion to avoid tissue damage.
Monitor the background and transient calcium signals during fine-tuning to confirm successful alignment with the target cell population.
Secure the optic fiber on the rat’s skull using dental cement and four anchor screws.
Wait until the dental cement has solidified.
Release the optic fiber then carefully lift up the arm of the adaptor.
Suture the wound closed.
Place the rat in a heated recovery cage.
Clean the fiber tip with 70% ethanol and a cotton swab before each recording.
Allow at least 1 week of recovery from the surgery before starting the imaging session.
Choose a fiber patch cord with low auto-fluorescence (LAF, Doric Lenses).
Perform photo-bleaching 1 hour prior to the recording session to minimize auto-fluorescent noise.
Select a region of interest only in the center of the fiber core if using a CMOS camera-based fiber photometry system.
Connect one end of the patch cord to the optical fiber output of a blue LED light source.
Place the opposite end of the patch cord in a beam dump or black box.
Set the output current of the light source to its maximum value.
Leave the light on for 1–2 hours.
Repeat the process for each patch cord if there are multiple channels.
Attach the low-auto fluorescent patch cable to the cannula tip on the rat’s head.
Record the baseline calcium activity.
Reduce the amount of light present in the recording room to a minimum.
Shelter the fiber cannula from environmental light using the Thorlabs interconnector.
If using other connectors, cover them with a black material such as heat-shrink tubing.
Ensure the DAQ system is grounded to avoid electrical noise contamination.
Visualize the collected fluorescent signals from the optic fiber in the DAQ software.
Apply a band-pass filter with low-cut at 0.1 Hz and high-cut at 100 Hz.
Use a 3 kHz sampling rate to reduce data size due to oversampling.
Refer to 'problem 8' if no fluorescent signal or only a very weak signal is detected during imaging.
Adjust the final output power of the LED to minimize bleaching effect.
Use an output power of 50–100 μW/mm² from the fiber tip with a 20 Hz stimulation rate.
Do not record continuously for more than 3 hours.
Photometry imaging can be conducted in awake and freely moving animals or while they are anesthetized.
For acute recording exclusively in anesthetized animals, no anchor screws are needed.
Imaging can begin immediately after implantation of the fiber cannula in the GCaMP6s-expressing region.
After recording, retract the optic fiber from the brain and wash with 70% ethanol for reuse.
Verify recording locations post-hoc using immuno-histological techniques.
Euthanize the rat using a single intra peritoneal injection of a ketamine/xylazine solution.
Perfuse the brain transcardially with phosphate-buffered saline followed by a 4% paraformaldehyde solution.
Decapitate the rat and dissect out the brain.
Post-fix the brain in 4% paraformaldehyde at 4°C with gentle agitation for 12 hours.
Cut the brain coronally into 50-μm thick sections using a vibratome.
Incubate the sections in blocking buffer (1×PBS + 1% Triton + 5% normal goat serum) for 2 hours at room temperature with gentle agitation.
Incubate the sections in primary solution (1×PBS + 1% Triton + primary antibodies) for 24–48 hours at 4°C with gentle agitation.
Wash the sections in 1×PBS (four washes, each lasting ten minutes) with gentle agitation.
Incubate the sections in secondary solution (1×PBS + 1% Triton + fluorescent secondary antibodies) for two hours at room temperature in the dark with gentle agitation.
Wash the sections in 1×PBS (four washes, each lasting ten minutes) with gentle agitation.
Mount sections on Superfrost Plus microscope glass slides, placing four sections per slide.
Allow the mounted sections to dry completely.
Cover the dried sections with glass coverslips (24 × 50 mm).
Acquire high-quality images of immuno-stained sections using a confocal laser-scanning microscope.
